summary.text: A previously healthy 14-year-old female presented to the emergency department with 12 hours of diffuse, cramping lower abdominal pain, progressive distension, 48 hours without passing feces or flatus, anorexia, nausea and one non-bilious vomiting episode, with no fever, no relevant prior history and no identifiable risk factors.

Examination showed an acutely ill, mildly distressed patient with stable vital signs, mild distension, hyperactive bowel sounds, a hyper-tympanic abdomen and mild lower abdominal tenderness greater in the left lower quadrant, without rigidity or rebound; rectal examination was unremarkable. Preoperative labs showed a mildly elevated WBC count with otherwise normal results.
Plain radiography showed a markedly dilated sigmoid colon with the coffee-bean sign, indicating large bowel obstruction from sigmoid volvulus, without free peritoneal air.

She received intravenous fluids and ceftriaxone and metronidazole, then underwent emergency laparotomy within two hours of presentation for severe and progressive symptoms and risk of bowel ischemia, which showed a redundant twisted sigmoid colon with preserved vascularity and no gangrene or perforation; the volvulus was reduced and the sigmoid colon was resected with primary end-to-end anastomosis. Histology was consistent with volvulus-related changes.
The postoperative course was uncomplicated; she was discharged on postoperative day 5 with scheduled follow-up and was asymptomatic and clinically stable at the two-week outpatient review.
